issues.issue: The effective date is left blank ("effective as of ____________"), yet Section 2.15 defines "Effective Date" as "the date first stated above" and dozens of deadlines run from it. The date the Agreement takes effect therefore cannot be fixed from the instrument's own words.

The recital fixes the project only in approximations ("approximately 124 communities", "approximately 1,392 community anchor institutions"), and those approximations feed the 90%-of-CAIs test in the Commencement Date definition. What counts as the denominator is not stated.

This recital that Network Operator "is experienced and skilled" could be argued to operate as a warranty of capability alongside the express warranties in Section 5.1.6 and 5.1.7. A court could be asked whether a recital creates obligations beyond Article 5.

The recital describes the services "among other things," an open-ended catch-all that sits against the specific enumeration of duties in Article 4 and the definition of "Services" in Section 2.60. A party could argue the recital enlarges the operative scope of work.

"Functions, responsibilities and tasks ... otherwise commonly performed by a dark fiber and lit network provider" imports unwritten industry duties with no stated benchmark. The phrase is vague and could be used to expand the Services beyond what Article 4 lists.

The rule that "all capitalized terms shall have the meanings set forth in this Article 2" fails when read against the rest of the instrument, which uses capitalized terms Article 2 never defines (e.g. "Attachment Database" in 4.3.4, "CAPEX Upgrade and Update Fund" in 4.9.6, "Termination Date" in 3.6.1.1, "Initial Plan" in 4.1.10.1, "Applicable Third Party" in 7.3.2). The definitional rule cannot be given effect as written.

This fixes the AAA Rules "in effect at the time a demand for arbitration is made," whereas the Guaranty Agreement's Section 4.6 elects AAA Commercial Rules "in effect on the date of the Agreement" and contemplates consolidation of the two proceedings. Which rule set governs a consolidated arbitration is unresolved.

"Control" is used three times to define Affiliate but is itself left undefined and carries no percentage or other threshold, unlike the 50% voting-securities test Section 8.1.4 supplies for change of control. The reach of "Affiliate" in Sections 4.8, 2.45 and 9.1 is therefore uncertain.

The definition points to "Section 4.9.2" for the Annual Plan, but Section 4.9.2 concerns agreements between MTC and third parties; the Annual Plan is actually required by Section 4.9.3.2. The cross-reference is wrong on its face.

MTC may revise the Exhibit A list of CAIs "in MTC's sole discretion up until the Commencement Date," while Section 2.8(a) makes the Commencement Date turn on 90% of "the CAIs" being connected. MTC can thus move the very target that determines when its own trigger is met.

Because the Commencement Date is "the earlier of" the 90% completion test or thirty months after the Effective Date, it arrives at thirty months even if the network is largely unbuilt, which is squarely the situation Section 4.9.2.8 addresses by merely reducing payments. Whether Network Operator's Commencement-Date obligations (e.g. the CAPEX payments under 4.9.6) nonetheless begin is left in doubt.

Confidential Information turns on what "would reasonably be understood by the Parties, to be proprietary or confidential," a standard with no boundary, and is expressly made subject to the Public Records Act. What is actually protected is indeterminate.

A Dark Fiber Customer is defined as a lessee "from MTC pursuant to Section 4.7.4," yet Section 4.7.4.4 contemplates a Dark Fiber Customer leasing from the Network Operator in its own name on a Network Operator Network Extension. The two cannot both be squared with the definition.
"The date first stated above" refers to the preamble, where the date is left blank. The Effective Date, from which nearly every deadline in Article 4 runs, cannot be determined from the document.

"Any financial statements of Network Operator delivered to MTC" defines the term by the act of delivery rather than by content, so it captures whatever is handed over. Its interaction with the specific statements required by Section 4.9.9 is unclear.

"Strikes" appear both in the unqualified enumerated list and again in the closing qualifier limiting them to strikes "not resulting from the responsible Party's ... failure to timely take necessary actions," so the same event is both automatically excused and conditionally excused. The threshold words "substantial and extraordinary" also supply no measurable boundary.

The Indemnifying Party is "the Party from which another person seeks or is entitled to indemnification," so mere assertion by any person makes a Party an Indemnifying Party. That is broader than Article 9, which imposes indemnity only between the two Parties.

KPIs are defined only as "any of the rating factors used to measure performance," with the actual indicators left to Exhibit E, which Section 4.13.1 admits the Parties are still "in the process of completing." The performance measures against which breach is judged are therefore not fixed by the instrument.

An MBI Network Extension must be "funded in whole or in part by MTC," yet Section 3.6.1.2(a) lets Network Operator claim credit for its own funds expended to construct "MBI Network Extensions" and Section 4.5.7 gives MTC ownership "regardless of the source of its funding." The funding element of the definition cannot be squared with those sections.

The MTC Network is defined to include "any MBI Network Extensions and IRUs," while Section 4.5.5 makes Network Operator Network Extensions the operator's sole property and Section 2.39 says an extension becomes part of the MTC Network unless the operator proves otherwise. The perimeter of the asset the operator must maintain is contestable.

The second sentence is circular: an extension "shall become part of the MTC Network unless it is a Network Extension and the Network Operator establishes to MTC's reasonable satisfaction that it is not or does not become part of the MTC Network." The test defines the result by reference to itself and gives no criteria.

A Network Operator Network Extension must be "funded and owned by the Network Operator" yet "excludes any Network Extension funded by MTC unless otherwise agreed," leaving jointly funded extensions unallocated. Section 4.5.7's rule that MTC owns MBI extensions "regardless of the source of its funding" makes the overlap worse.

Deemed fees are measured by what a third party would pay "for similar services on the MTC Network," and "similar" is given no benchmark beyond a single illustrative example. The amount of phantom revenue on which revenue sharing is computed is therefore indeterminate.

After enumerating specific policies, the definition adds "any additional policies reasonably required by MTC to meet legal requirements," an open-ended catch-all that MTC may populate unilaterally while Section 4.12 demands "full compliance with all Network Policies." The enumerated list and the catch-all pull against each other.

The definition enumerates four revenue sources in (a)–(d) and then sweeps in "any amounts earned by Network Operator from services related to the MTC Network, other than the categories expressly excluded," so the enumerated list and the catch-all cannot both be given full effect. Whether a given receipt is Network Revenue, on which revenue sharing and the CAPEX and decommissioning payments turn, is open.

A Network Segment is whatever MTC defines during construction "and thereafter by mutual agreement," leaving no segment boundaries fixed if the parties do not agree. Section 3.6.1.5(b) prices the dark fiber option by "the highest number of strands leased in any Network Segment," so the undefined unit drives money.

An Officer's Certificate is said to have contents "binding upon the entity," a phrase that does not say whether it is a warranty, an estoppel, or merely evidence. Its effect where a certificate later proves inaccurate (Sections 3.6.1.2, 4.9.9.4) is unspecified.

Price Caps are said to be "the prices set forth in Exhibit F," but the Agreement's exhibit list assigns Price Caps to Exhibit D and makes Exhibit F the Master Services Agreement with EOPSS and ITD. The definition points to the wrong exhibit.

The carve-out says Network Operator Network Extension prices are in its "sole discretion" except that bandwidth charges to MassDOT, ITD or EOPSS are "governed by Section 4.7.2," but 4.7.2 caps those charges at 85% of the Price Schedule, which by this same definition does not apply to extensions. The two provisions cannot both be applied to an extension customer.

A Renewal Decision must conform to "the requirements of Section 3.2," but Section 3.2 states no requirements for any decision and the defined term appears nowhere else in the Agreement. The definition is unanchored.

Retail Service is defined solely by the identity of the provider — "services provided by a Third Party Service Provider" — which makes Section 4.8's prohibition on the Network Operator providing Retail Services impossible to breach as a matter of definition. The definition and the operative prohibition cannot both be given effect.

"Services" means "all performance obligations of the Network Operator hereunder," a wholly circular definition that Section 4.7.1 then extends to unwritten tasks "deemed to be implied." What is and is not a Service is not determinable from the term itself.

The SLA definition describes a document whose substance is left to Exhibit E, which Section 4.13.1 concedes is still being completed and is not attached. The service levels the definition presupposes do not exist in the instrument.

"Term" runs "until the expiration or termination of this Agreement," but Section 8.4.1 provides that neither the Term nor the operator's obligations "shall be deemed to have expired or terminated" until services transfer assistance is complete. Whether the Term ends on the date fixed by Section 3.1 or is extended indefinitely by 8.4.1 is unresolved.

The definition sweeps in "any organization other than Network Operator providing retail broadband service," which on its face includes an Affiliate of the Network Operator that Section 4.8 permits to be a Third Party Service Provider. The scope of the enumerated carrier categories versus the general opening words is contestable.

Clause (c) makes "lit transmission service of not less than 10 Gbps to an institutional customer" a Wholesale Service, which permits the Network Operator to serve an end user directly notwithstanding Section 4.8's prohibition on its providing Retail Services. The boundary between the two is unstable.

The Term "will terminate upon the tenth (10th) anniversary of the Commencement Date," yet Section 8.4.1 says the Term shall not be deemed expired or terminated until services transfer assistance is completed or waived by MTC. The two provisions give different end dates for the same Term.

Renewal is "by mutual agreement of the parties," yet Section 2.54 defines a "Renewal Decision" as a written MTC decision "conforming to the requirements of Section 3.2" — requirements this Section does not contain. What Section 3.2 requires of MTC in responding to a Renewal Request cannot be determined.

A Renewal Request may be made only "within the period from thirty (30) to thirty-two (32) months prior to the expiration" with time of the essence, and the section says nothing about the consequence of a request made outside that two-month window. Whether a late request is void or merely voidable is unaddressed.

Either Party may walk away from renewal negotiations after the 28-month date, but Sections 3.6.1.3 and 3.6.1.4 attach very different dark-fiber pricing consequences to which Party "notifies" the other that it does not wish to renew. Terminating negotiations under 3.4 without such a notification leaves the pricing branch unassigned.

The rights are granted only "upon expiration of the Term," although the heading of Section 3.6 is "Upon Termination or Expiration" and Section 3.6.2 addresses termination for cause; what happens on a termination that is neither expiration nor MTC-for-cause (e.g. under 8.6 or 8.3.1) is not stated. The trigger for the option is ambiguous.
The right is to lease "between four (4) and eight (8) strands" without saying who elects the number within that range or on what basis. The quantity term of the option is left indeterminate.

The net-operating-loss measuring period runs "until the last calendar quarter before the date of the Request for Renewal," but no term "Request for Renewal" is defined (Section 2.55 defines "Renewal Request") and Section 3.6.1.3(d) contemplates that no such request is ever made. In that case the calculation has no end date.

Clause (c) triggers this pricing table simply "upon the expiry of the Term of this Agreement," which occurs in every case, so this table would always apply and would displace the different, less favourable table Section 3.6.1.4 prescribes when the Network Operator declines to renew. The two sections cannot both be given effect.

This table applies where Network Operator declines renewal, but Section 3.6.1.3(c) makes its own table applicable "upon the expiry of the Term" in all events, and the two produce different exercise prices on the same facts. Which controls is not stated.

The adjustment refers to "the per strand rate stated in Section 3.6.1.3 or 3.1.6.4," and there is no Section 3.1.6.4 — the evident intended reference is 3.6.1.4. The mis-citation leaves the second pricing table arguably unadjusted for CPI.

This prices the option on "the highest number of strands leased in any Network Segment regardless of disclaimers of use made pursuant to Section 3.6.1.11," while 3.6.1.11 provides that disclaimed strands are excluded and all rights in them become void. Whether a disclaimer reduces what the operator pays cannot be answered consistently.

Payment is due "on or before the end of the Term," yet Section 3.6.1 makes the rights arise only "upon expiration of the Term" and conditions them on NTIA approval that may not yet exist. The operator is required to pay before it is known whether the option exists.

"Total discounts available under this Section shall not exceed $6,000,000" does not say whether "this Section" is 3.6.1.7, 3.6.1, or all of 3.6, nor whether the cap is per strand or in the aggregate, though the tables in 3.6.1.3 can generate dollar-for-dollar discounts far exceeding that figure. The cap's field of operation is ambiguous.

The 25-year lease commences "upon termination or expiration of the Term," although Section 3.6.1 grants the underlying right only upon expiration and Section 3.6.2 denies it upon termination for cause. The commencement trigger does not match the trigger for the right itself.

New extensions and connections must comply with "MTC's policies then applicable to others" and fees "at then-prevailing prices," neither of which is fixed or constrained by any standard of reasonableness. The post-term cost of the leased fiber is left to MTC's later policy-making.

The maintenance baseline is "half the actual maintenance costs ... during the last two full calendar year prior to the exercise," which is grammatically broken and does not say whether the figure is the average of the two years or their total. The pro rata formula that follows is applied to a baseline that cannot be computed with confidence.

Disclaimed strands are excluded from the operator's pro rata cost shares here, but Section 3.6.1.5(b) fixes the total exercise price on the highest strand count "regardless of disclaimers of use made pursuant to Section 3.6.1.11." The effect of a disclaimer differs between the two provisions.

It is unclear whether the trailing condition "and the Network Operator has invested less than $3,000,000" qualifies only clause (b) or both clauses (a) and (b), which decides whether a for-cause termination alone defeats the Dark Fiber Rights. The syntax of the compound condition is genuinely ambiguous.

Network Operator is made "responsible for all aspects" of the network and the enumerated duties are stated to be its responsibilities "generally," so the specific list in 4.1.1–4.1.9 sits against an unbounded general obligation. Whether an unlisted cost or task falls within the operator's duties is left open.

Section 4.1.10.1 requires a draft of the capitalized "Initial Plan" pursuant to Section 4.9.3.1, but no "Initial Plan" is defined in Article 2 and 4.9.3.1 speaks only of an "initial plan." The deliverable's required content is fixed only by the loose narrative description in 4.9.3.1.

Deadlines are to be "reasonably adjusted" for MTC-caused information delays, with no mechanism, no measure and no decision-maker specified. Whether an adjustment has occurred, and by how much, is left at large.

MTC is "solely responsible for design, engineering, installation and construction decisions," yet Section 4.9.2.9 has MTC agree only to "seek advice" and take "commercially reasonable steps" so the network is built to let the operator meet the Agreement's parameters. Where a design defect prevents SLA performance, the allocation of responsibility between these two sections is contestable.

Marketing and advance sales must begin "promptly after the Effective Date" and be reported "in such detail as MTC may reasonably request," neither of which is measurable. What constitutes compliance before any network exists is undefined.

A Party is "deemed to have accepted" test results unless it challenges within five business days, yet MTC need give the seven-day notice only "when doing so will not adversely impact the construction schedule." Whether deemed acceptance operates where no notice was given is not answered.

Network Operator must perform additional services on MTC's demand while the Parties "shall negotiate an amendment hereto that affords commercially reasonable terms" — an agreement to agree on the price of work already required. The compensation term is unenforceably open.

The duty to assist with "all information, material, documentation, and reports that may be reasonably required or requested by MTC" is open-ended and unpriced. Its outer limit against the cost allocation in Section 4.9.1 is not drawn.

The Ramp-Up Plan requires "approval by MTC, EOPSS and ITD," making Network Operator's performance depend on the consent of entities that are not Parties and on whom Section 12.11 confers no rights. What happens if EOPSS or ITD withholds approval is unaddressed.

This passage is cast as what "the Parties intend" and what ITD and EOPSS "will be responsible for," rather than as an obligation of either Party, leaving it unclear whether it is operative at all. The demarcation-point allocation on which it turns is itself left to the Fiber Management Plan.

Segment-by-segment responsibilities commence on acceptance testing, whereas Section 4.2.1 makes MTC solely responsible until the Commencement Date and Section 4.9.6 keys the operator's capital payments to the Commencement Date. When the operator's duties and payments actually start is not consistently stated.

The disclaimer refers to "the Contract Price earned by Design-Build Contractor," a capitalized term defined nowhere in this Agreement and drawn from a contract to which Network Operator is not a party. Its scope cannot be fixed from this instrument.

Network Operator takes over the Attachment Database only "beginning on the Commencement Date," yet Section 4.1.2 lists maintaining records in the Attachment Database among its general responsibilities without that limitation. The two provisions give different start dates for the same duty.

Network Operator must "develop" and submit "all Network Policies," but Section 2.44 defines Network Policies to include MTC's own Open Access Policy, FCC policies and a federal highway policy that the operator cannot author. The obligation cannot be squared with the defined term it uses.

The Fiber Management Plan draft is due "within six (6) months after execution of this Agreement," while Section 4.1.10.4 sets the same deliverable at six months "of the Effective Date." Execution and the Effective Date need not coincide, so the two deadlines can differ.

The section states only conditions on which MTC "will not approve" the plan, and criteria such as "excessive stranded segments of fiber" and consistency with "MBI's legislatively stated mission" have no defined content. Nothing obliges MTC to approve a conforming plan, leaving Section 4.5.2 without a completion mechanism.

The carve-out "except as otherwise expressly provided in this Section" does not say whether "this Section" means 4.5.4 alone or all of 4.5, which matters because Section 4.5.5 does give the operator ownership of its own extensions. The scope of the no-ownership rule is ambiguous.

Network Operator Network Extensions are declared "the sole property of the Network Operator," while Section 2.39 provides that an extension "shall become part of the MTC Network" unless the operator establishes otherwise to MTC's reasonable satisfaction. Ownership of the same facility is addressed by two rules that pull in opposite directions.

The Network Operator must engage "one or more qualified contractors" with no standard of qualification stated and no allocation of who bears the cost of the Interconnection work. Both are left to be supplied from outside the text.

Wholesale Customer-funded extensions are "the sole property of such Wholesale Customer or its designee," yet Section 2.39 makes any fiber optic cable extension part of the MTC Network unless the Network Operator proves otherwise. Nothing reconciles customer ownership with that default.

MTC "shall own any MBI Network Extension, regardless of the source of its funding," while Section 2.36 defines an MBI Network Extension as one "funded in whole or in part by MTC." The ownership rule and the definition describe different sets of facilities.

Network Operator "is required to periodically update or upgrade" the network to maintain carrier-grade quality, yet the same section funds all such work solely from the CAPEX Upgrade and Update Fund and caps even MTC-directed expenditures at the Fund's available balance. Whether the upgrade duty survives an exhausted Fund is unresolved.

Tasks "whether or not specifically described in this Agreement" are "deemed to be implied by and included within the scope of the Services" if required for their proper performance, which sets an unbounded catch-all against the detailed enumeration of duties in Article 4. What falls inside the Services is decided by a standard the clause does not supply.

Rates must not exceed "the Price Caps in Exhibit F," but the Agreement's exhibit list makes Exhibit D the Price Caps and Exhibit F the EOPSS/ITD Master Services Agreement, and the proviso then measures government rates against 85% of the Price Schedule rather than the caps. The rate ceiling actually applicable to MassDOT, EOPSS and ITD is indeterminate.

Third Party Service Provider contracts are assigned to MTC with effect "upon termination of this Agreement," while Section 8.5.1 provides that on expiration or termination such third party agreements are transferred only "on mutually acceptable terms and conditions" and at MTC's request. The automatic assignment and the negotiated transfer cannot both govern.

The price is fixed "at a the price of $60/mile/strand/month" but is simultaneously said to be the fee "pursuant to the Pricing Schedule, as the same may be adjusted from time to time" — and no "Pricing Schedule" is defined (Section 2.53 defines "Price Schedule"). Whether $60 is a fixed price or a floating schedule rate is unclear.

A fully conforming lease request must still be presented "to MTC for approval of the lease," with no standard governing MTC's decision, which sits awkwardly with the Open Access and non-discrimination policies incorporated by Section 2.44. Whether MTC may refuse a compliant request is unaddressed.

The Parties merely "will develop guidelines" for non-standard leases, with an "expectation" of accommodation and "favorable consideration" — precatory language creating no ascertainable obligation. Whether a refusal breaches this section cannot be determined from its terms.

Where the leased dark fiber is on a Network Operator Network Extension "contiguous with the dark fiber on the MTC Network," the operator contracts in its own name, but Section 4.7.4.5 requires a 50/50 split of payments for dark fiber on the MTC Network. A single contiguous lease straddling both is not allocated between the sections.

Only payments received "during the Term of this Agreement" are split 50/50, although an IRU is by nature a long-term instrument whose payments may fall due after the Term ends. Who takes post-Term IRU payments is not stated.

The Price Schedule must be consistent with "the Price Caps as set forth in Exhibit F, as amended from time to time pursuant to ARTICLE 6," but Article 6 gives the IPT only a recommending function and Section 6.2 requires a negotiated amendment for material pricing changes. How Price Caps are actually amended is left unclear.

This allows "the Price Schedules, including the Price Caps" to be updated annually with MTC's approval, whereas Section 12.1 permits modifications of the Agreement (of which the Price Caps exhibit is part) only "by a written document signed by both Parties." Whether an approved annual update amends the Agreement is unresolved.

The prohibition "Network Operator shall not provide Retail Services" is empty as drafted, because Section 2.57 defines Retail Service as "services provided by a Third Party Service Provider," a category that by Section 2.64 excludes the Network Operator. The prohibition and the definition cannot both be given effect.

The obligation to pay "all ongoing costs of operating the MTC Network ... and all costs of compliance with the terms of this Agreement" is followed by a long enumeration and then the catch-all "all other operating and monitoring expenses contemplated by this Agreement," against carve-outs for design and construction funding. Which side of that line a given cost falls on — and how far the funding duty extends — is contestable.

Exhibit I agreements are furnished "for informational purposes only," while Section 4.9.2.3 imposes administration responsibilities as to future agreements of essentially the same kind. Whether an Exhibit I agreement can later become one the operator must administer is not addressed.

The operator will have "the responsibilities described in this Agreement" with respect to Exhibit J agreements "when executed," without identifying which responsibilities or fixing the terms of agreements still in draft. The obligation assumed is unascertainable from the text.

This binds Network Operator to responsibilities under agreements MTC has not yet made, described only as ones "aimed at maintaining or enhancing the extent, structure, functioning and viability of the MTC Network" and "including but not limited to" property access agreements. The general words have no boundary against the specific examples given.

The estimate is made "a precondition to exercising the right to object set forth in Section 4.9.2.5," but Section 4.9.2.5 confers no right to object — it grants only a credit against revenue sharing. The precondition refers to a right that does not exist in the cited section.

The credit is for costs incurred "as a result of MTC's agreeing to the contractual term objected to," yet Section 4.9.2.4 requires only a written estimate and identification of differing terms and creates no objection procedure. Whether an objection was ever made, and what one is, cannot be determined between the two sections.

"This Subsection" is undefined — it may mean 4.9.2.6, 4.9.2.5, or the whole of 4.9.2 — so the reach of the mandatory dispute resolution referral is unclear. Nothing else in the section identifies the intended unit.

The operator acts as MTC's agent but expressly lacks authority to terminate, modify or waive anything under the third party agreements, while Section 4.1.9 makes it "administratively responsible for ensuring compliance with all of the requirements of such agreements." Responsibility without corresponding authority is a tension the Agreement does not resolve.

Payments are reduced "in proportion to the average shortfall (from 90%) in the percentage of CAIs that have been connected as of the end of each week during that period," a formula that does not say whether the reduction is proportional to the shortfall or to the connected percentage. The arithmetic of the relief cannot be performed with confidence.

MTC "represents and agrees" it will take commercially reasonable steps to have the network designed and built so the operator can meet the Agreement's parameters, while Section 4.2.1 makes MTC "solely responsible" for design decisions and leaves the operator only a right to comment. Where a design shortfall defeats SLA performance, which section governs is open.

This requires an "initial plan" whose only content requirement is a narrative, while Section 4.1.10.1 calls the same deliverable a capitalized "Initial Plan." The document's required contents and status as a defined deliverable are inconsistent between the two sections.

This is the provision that actually requires the Annual Plan, yet Section 2.4 defines "Annual Plan" as the plan submitted "pursuant to Section 4.9.2," a different subsection dealing with third party agreements. The defined term and its operative source do not match.

The fee schedule runs by "Year 1" through "Year 10" without saying whether a Year is measured from the Effective Date or the Commencement Date, though the Term itself ends on the tenth anniversary of the Commencement Date and payments commence with the Effective Date. Which year's rate applies in any given quarter is therefore uncertain.

The Year 1 rate "shall be paid on the Effective Date" ratably for the partial quarter, which does not sit with the main rule in Section 4.9.4 that the fee is paid "in four (4) equal parts at the beginning of each calendar quarter." Whether the first payment is a whole quarter or a prorated stub is contestable.

The formula multiplies the Year 10 fee by "100 plus the increase in CPI ... stated as a percentage," but the worked example converts a 15-point rise (150 to 165) into a multiplier of 110%, which the stated formula does not produce. The text and its own illustration give different answers.

The section directs "a determination of CPI Escalation," a capitalized term that appears nowhere else and is defined nowhere in Article 2. What is being determined, and by what measure, is left to inference.

Revenue sharing is computed on "Network Revenue attributable to that fiscal year," while Section 2.45 defines Network Revenue as revenue "recognized" under IFRS during the Term. Attribution and recognition are not the same test, and the difference decides which year's band applies.

MTC may divert "amounts in the Fund [that] exceed the amounts reasonably required for the purposes of the Fund," without any method for determining that amount, even though Section 4.6.1 makes the same Fund the only source of the operator's mandatory upgrade obligations. The size of the surplus is left to assertion.

MTC may in "its sole discretion" apply the decommissioning fund to "any purpose consistent with MBI's legislatively stated mission," a mission the Agreement nowhere identifies, while the operator's 2% payments continue regardless. The limit on MTC's use of the money is unascertainable from the instrument.

The statements must reflect "all Network Operator's assets, liabilities, income expenses, not limited to those related to the MTC Network" — a garbled enumeration that leaves it unclear whether income and expenses are one item or two and how far beyond the MTC Network the disclosure reaches. The scope of the reporting duty turns on that broken phrase.

The officer must certify absolutely that "there has been no fraud or intentional or willful misconduct by any Person," without any knowledge qualifier and using a capitalized "Person" that Article 2 does not define. The certification is broader than any officer could truthfully give.

The restriction covers contracts "having a stated duration of more than two (2) years for which application of IFRS would call for recognition of revenue ... more than two (2) years after actual receipt," and it is not clear whether both conditions must be met or the second merely explains the first. Whether an ordinary three-year wholesale contract needs consent turns on that reading.

Maintenance must comply with specifications "contained or incorporated, or to be contained or incorporated, in MTC's agreement with its Design-Build Contractor" — a document the operator is not party to and whose future contents are unknown — and with "the standards for carrier class networks." The governing standard is not ascertainable from this Agreement.

"Appropriate Scheduled Maintenance" is measured by Network Operator's "then current preventative maintenance procedures, which shall meet or exceed standard industry practice," letting the obligor set its own standard. "Standard industry practice" is given no content.

On cancellation or delay the operator "will comply with the provisions of the previous sentence to reschedule any delayed activity," but the immediately previous sentence concerns MTC's right to be present, not coordination or rescheduling. The cross-reference points to the wrong sentence.

Emergency Unscheduled Maintenance and Non-Emergency Unscheduled Maintenance overlap, since an "event imminently likely to cause" failure under 4.11.4.1 is also a "potential service-affecting situation" under 4.11.4.2, and only the latter carries a reporting deadline. Which category governs a given event is not determinable.

"Workmanlike care" is a lower and different standard from the warranty in Section 5.1.8 that the Services will be performed "in accordance with or exceeding generally accepted industry standards." Which standard governs maintenance work is not stated.

The operator must "apply any proceeds of such claims to the repair or replacement of the damaged property," while Section 10.3.4 names MTC as loss payee on the property policies and MTC owns the network. Who controls and receives the proceeds is answered differently by the two provisions.

Rental loss proceeds count as Network Revenue only "net of legal fees or other extraordinary costs of recovery," whereas Section 2.45 requires Network Revenue to be calculated "on a gross basis, without deductions or allowances" and expressly includes rental loss proceeds. The two measures of the same receipt conflict.

The operator must respond "as quickly as possible" with an allowance for circumstances beyond its reasonable control, a standard that does not align with the fixed restoration intervals contemplated by the SLAs and the MassDOT Operating Agreement referenced in the same sentence. Which measure governs a late restoration is unclear.

The operator may subcontract "any of the maintenance services hereunder," which sits against Section 12.10's bar on assigning the Agreement "in whole or in part" without consent. Where wholesale subcontracting shades into a partial assignment is not addressed.

MTC may direct testing "no more frequently than every five (5) years," a limit that sits against Section 4.14.1's right of access "at all reasonable times" to verify "the integrity of the operational status of the MTC Network." Whether MTC may effectively compel testing more often through its audit right is unresolved.

"Full compliance with all Network Policies" is required, but Section 2.44 lets MTC add "any additional policies reasonably required by MTC" at any time, and breach of this section is a ground for termination under Section 8.1.1. The obligation's content can be enlarged unilaterally after signature.

Performance is measured against "the SLA the Parties are in the process of completing," a document that is not attached and whose Exhibit E is blank. The central performance standard of the Agreement is left to future agreement.

The Parties "will review and agree to commercially reasonable changes" to the performance standards, an agreement to agree with no fallback if they do not. What happens on disagreement is left to a good-faith duty and nothing more.

Performance is measured against KPIs "as the same may evolve and be supplemented and enhanced during the Term," without saying who may change them or by what process. The measure of compliance is a moving and unowned target.

On an audit finding of incorrect accounting the operator must "promptly make all remunerative payments to MTC" — a word that has no settled meaning in this context and appears to be an error for corrective or remedial payments. The provision also says nothing about amounts found owing to the operator.

The operator must make "any changes and take other actions which are necessary" to maintain legal and Network Policy compliance, at unlimited cost and with no materiality or cost threshold. The boundary against Section 4.9.1's cost allocation is undrawn.

The carve-out reads "unless expressly constructed otherwise," evidently an error for "construed," and the limited-license characterization must also accommodate the IRU leasehold the operator may acquire under Section 3.6. The words as written do not say what displaces the license characterization.

The operator must supply and pay for all resources "necessary or appropriate" for the Services, a disjunctive standard in which "appropriate" has no limit. Read with Section 4.7.1's implied-services clause, the cost exposure is unbounded.

"An adequate number of trained and qualified personnel" sets no headcount, qualification or staffing benchmark other than the NOC's 24x7 requirement elsewhere. Adequacy is left to be judged after the fact.

MTC gives only "reasonable access" here, while Section 4.16.1 states that "MTC authorizes Network Operator all access to its facilities and premises needed to support the Services." The two grants of access are of different scope.

The Massachusetts office "shall be the headquarters for the Network Operator" without saying whether that means headquarters for the MTC Network operations or the corporate headquarters of the entity itself. The obligation assumed is materially different on the two readings.

Background check policies must be "no less stringent than the then-current requirements of MassDOT, ITD and EOPSS," requirements set by non-parties that may change at any time and are not annexed. The standard of compliance is not fixed by the Agreement.

The Network Operator warrants that "this Agreement constitutes a legal, valid and binding obligation" as of the Effective Date, while Section 12.14 provides the Agreement "shall become binding only upon condition" that the parent delivers an acceptable guaranty. The two cannot both be true at signature.

This is a warranty of historical facts "at all times since January 1, 2005," yet the chapeau of Section 5.1 makes every warranty speak "as of the Effective Date and continuing throughout the Term." A past-fact representation cannot sensibly be made continuing, and it extends to a non-party parent company.

The warranty of having "successfully provided and performed the Services or services that are substantially equivalent ... in other settings and circumstances" has no benchmark for success or equivalence. Whether it was breached cannot be tested against any stated measure.

Performance is warranted to meet "generally accepted industry standards," while Section 4.13.1 measures the same Services against the standards of an SLA that is not yet written. Which standard governs a performance failure is unresolved.

Network Operator warrants it holds all approvals applicable to "the operation of the MTC Network," a network MTC owns and for which MTC and MassDOT hold the underlying property and highway rights. Which authorizations are the operator's responsibility is not delimited.

The covenant to cooperate "to effect the goals, objectives and purposes of this Agreement" in a "commercially reasonable manner" states no ascertainable duty. It could be invoked to require conduct nowhere else specified.

The covenant against any transaction that "would constitute self-dealing" leaves that term undefined, while Section 4.8 expressly contemplates the operator contracting with its own Affiliate and Section 2.43 deems fees on its own extensions. What is prohibited self-dealing and what is permitted Affiliate dealing is not drawn.

Compliance is promised with "Article 5 of the Master Services Agreement between MTC and EOPSS and ITD," a document the same sentence admits is "currently being negotiated." The content of the obligation does not exist at signature.

The operator represents as of the Effective Date that it "has taken out all insurance required under this Agreement," but Section 10.3.3 allows thirty days after the Effective Date for certificates and permits certain coverages to be procured later with MTC's consent. The representation and the insurance timetable do not match.

The operator must "ensure that the MTC Network is and remains" compliant with all laws and Network Policies — an absolute guarantee about an asset MTC owns, designs and builds under Section 4.2.1. The warranty is broader than the operator's control of the subject matter.

Notice must be given "immediately" of any event rendering the warranties incorrect, without a defined period, and several of those warranties (such as Section 5.1.5) are historical facts that no later event can render incorrect. The trigger and timing of the notice duty are both indeterminate.

MTC warrants the Agreement is a binding obligation "as of the Effective Date," while Section 12.14 makes the Agreement binding only on delivery of an acceptable parent guaranty. The warranty and the condition precedent are inconsistent.

The IPT is given the purpose "to resolve disputes submitted by the Parties pursuant to ARTICLE 11," but under Section 11.1.2 the IPT is merely a fifteen-day way station before escalation and arbitration and has no power to decide anything. The resolution function stated here has no counterpart in Article 11.

The IPT includes "one person representing jointly EOPSS and ITD," who is not a representative of either Party, yet Section 11.1.3 lets the IPT stay the arbitration timetable "upon unanimous vote of its members." That gives a non-party a veto over the Parties' dispute resolution clock.

The IPT need "meet at least once a year," while Section 11.1.1.2 requires it to meet "as often as necessary" and Section 11.1.2 gives it only fifteen days to resolve a submitted dispute. The standing meeting obligation does not support the dispute function assigned to it.

Where IPT recommendations are material the Parties "may either negotiate to amend the Agreement ... or consider the change during any subsequent renewal," which obliges neither Party to do anything, yet Section 4.7.5.2 allows the Price Caps themselves to be updated annually with MTC's approval alone. The two routes to changing pricing cannot both be the governing one.

Either Party may demand "at any time" that all Confidential Information be "promptly deliver[ed]" back, which would strip the Network Operator of information the same sentence licenses it to hold "as required to perform the Services." The return right and the performance licence collide within the section.

This subordinates confidentiality to the Public Records Act and to compulsory process, while Section 2.9 and Section 7.1 declare the same material to be the exclusive property of the disclosing party. What protection Confidential Information actually enjoys in MTC's hands is left to Exhibits H-1 and H-2 and to statute.

Network Operator must comply with MTC's confidentiality policies "as communicated by MTC's Executive Director or General Counsel to Network Operator from time to time," which lets MTC add obligations unilaterally, whereas Section 12.1 permits modifications only by a document signed by both Parties. The two provisions cannot both govern later-communicated policies.

The exception turns on direction "by the General Counsel," a person identified nowhere in the Agreement's definitions, and the prohibition runs in favour of "any Person" — another undefined capitalized term. Who must authorize a disclosure is not fixed by the text.

The clause bars use for the benefit of "any Person related to or that is an Affiliate of with Network Operator" — a garbled phrase — and protects "any Applicable Third Party," a capitalized term the Agreement never defines. Both the class of prohibited beneficiaries and the class of protected persons are unascertainable.

The section requires delivery of "all copies of MTC's Written Materials," a capitalized term defined nowhere, and imposes indemnity "to the maximum extent required by law," which is not the usual "permitted by law" and has no evident meaning. Both the property to be returned and the extent of the indemnity are uncertain.

The Parties must cooperate on any statement "relating to or bearing on the work performed or data collected under this Agreement," a scope broad enough to capture routine customer communications, subject only to a carve-out for regulatory reporting. The boundary of the approval requirement is not drawn.

The exceptions are expressed to qualify only "Network Operator's obligations under Section 7.3," leaving the ownership and return obligations in Section 7.1 and the Exhibit H obligations in Section 7.2 without any public-domain or compelled-disclosure carve-out. Whether the carve-outs extend to the rest of Article 7 is open.

Article 8 nowhere uses or defines termination "for cause," yet Sections 3.6.1 and 3.6.2 make the Network Operator's entire Dark Fiber Rights turn on whether "MTC terminates this Agreement for cause." Which of the grounds in 8.1.1 through 8.1.4 count as cause is not stated.

The deferral charge escalates for each thirty-day period "beyond the initial thirty (30) days that the breach remains uncured," but Sections 8.1.2 and 8.1.3 supply no notice-and-cure period at all, so the formula has no starting point for those grounds. The charge cannot be computed for the very breaches it is said to cover.

Termination requires "a disruption to the basic functioning of more than fifty percent (50%) of the MTC Network," without saying whether the fifty percent is measured in route miles, strands, CAIs, customers or revenue. The threshold cannot be applied as written.

Force majeure relief is available only for an event occurring "after the Commencement Date," leaving the operator with no excuse for a Force Majeure Event during the up to thirty months of pre-Commencement obligations imposed by Sections 4.1.10, 4.2.3 and 4.9.4. The gap is created by the section's own words.

"Neither the Term ... nor Network Operator's obligations ... shall be deemed to have expired or terminated until the services transfer assistance ... is completed or MTC waives the requirement," which cannot be squared with Section 3.1's fixed termination on the tenth anniversary of the Commencement Date or with the definition of Term in Section 2.63. On its face it lets MTC extend the operator's obligations indefinitely.

The duty to provide transfer assistance for up to twelve months before expiration, or on any notice of termination, says nothing about who bears its cost or what the assistance consists of beyond "as described herein." Neither the content nor the compensation of the obligation is fixed.

"Upon request by MTC, the effective date of such expiration or termination shall be extended for up to one year" gives MTC a unilateral extension power, whereas Section 3.2 permits extension only "by mutual agreement of the parties" for defined Renewal Terms. The two mechanisms for prolonging the relationship conflict.

Third party agreements are transferred at termination only "on mutually acceptable terms and conditions" and at MTC's request, while Section 4.7.3 effects an immediate present assignment of Third Party Service Provider contracts effective on termination. The same contracts are dealt with by two inconsistent mechanisms.

Network Operator may terminate for MTC's material breach or insolvency, but Section 3.6.1 grants the Dark Fiber Rights only "upon expiration of the Term" and Section 3.6.2 addresses only MTC's for-cause termination. What becomes of the operator's option after its own rightful termination is unaddressed.

The indemnity is limited to the five enumerated categories (a)–(e), which cover third party claims and non-compliance but not the operator's own breach of this Agreement, so whether MTC's direct losses are indemnified turns on the closed list. The enumeration and the opening words "all claims, liabilities, costs, or expenses arising out of" pull in different directions.

The Indemnifying Party controls the defence only "so long as [it] is not in default in the performance of its obligations under the Agreement," without limiting that to material or related defaults. Any alleged default could be used to strip control of the defence.

Any settlement requires "the written approval of both the Parties," which cannot be squared with Section 9.3's grant to the Indemnifying Party of "primary responsibility for the conduct of an Indemnified Claim Proceeding and the defense." Neither section says what happens when approval is refused.

The contractual liability coverage is required to cover "any insurable indemnity obligations under Section 9.1(a), 9.1(d) or 9.1(e)," pointedly omitting 9.1(b) and 9.1(c), while the opening words add "such other coverages as the Parties may determine are commercially reasonable." Whether the omission of two indemnity heads is deliberate is a question the clause invites.

The property coverage the operator must buy is whatever the Parties later "confer" and use "commercially reasonable efforts to agree" upon, with no default level, type or limit if they do not agree. The core property insurance obligation is an agreement to agree.

Earth movement coverage must apply "regardless of any other cause or event contributing concurrently or in any other sequence of Losses," using a capitalized "Losses" that is defined nowhere in the Agreement. The intended anti-concurrent-causation effect is expressed through an undefined term.

The aggregate limit requirement applies only "where possible" and must be "commensurate with the value of the assets in service, or such other value as MTC may approve," which fixes no number and no method. Whether a given limit complies cannot be determined from the text.

Coverage for MTC property in transit or storage is required only "within limits reasonably determined by Network Operator and MTC," leaving the limits to later agreement with no fallback. The obligation is incomplete on its face.

The rental loss cover is required only "subject to such further determination as to commercially reasonable amounts, timing, deductibles, and terms," while Section 2.45 already counts its proceeds as Network Revenue owed in part to MTC. Whether any rental loss cover is actually mandatory is left to a later determination that may never occur.

Network Operator "waives all rights to recover against MTC" for insured loss or damage to its property, which sits against MTC's indemnity of the operator in Section 9.2 for MTC's own contract breaches and legal non-compliance. Whether the waiver defeats an otherwise indemnified claim is unresolved.

The section allows that "certain types of insurance are not required within thirty (30) days of the Effective Date" without identifying which, and requires certificates "within five (5) days of requiring such insurance" — a phrase that does not say what triggers the requirement. Compliance is a condition whose scope cannot be determined, and breach carries a ten-day termination right under Section 8.1.1.

MTC "shall be named as loss payee as its interest may appear on the property insurance policies," while Section 4.11.8.1 requires Network Operator to prosecute the property claims and apply the proceeds itself, subject to MTC approval only above $500,000. Who receives and controls insurance proceeds is answered differently in the two sections.

The additional insurance obligation is measured by "agreements between MTC and others that are within the scope of Section 4.1," but Section 4.1 is a general overview of the operator's responsibilities and identifies no agreements; the third party agreements are dealt with in Section 4.9.2. The cross-reference does not identify the agreements it invokes.

This makes Article 11 the exclusive route for "any dispute between the Parties," whereas the Guaranty Agreement's Section 4.6 gives MTC an election between AAA arbitration and litigation in Middlesex County and purports to incorporate "all other provisions relating to dispute resolution" from this Agreement. How the mandatory clause here operates alongside the guarantor's elective clause is contestable.

The officers are given until thirty days after receipt of the Dispute Resolution Notice to resolve the dispute, yet Section 11.1.3 permits arbitration only if it is unresolved "within forty-five (45) days after the receipt of the Dispute Resolution Notice." The two provisions leave a fifteen-day gap with no stated status.

The section speaks only of "the decision or award" being final, binding and non-appealable and entered as a judgment, and says nothing about interim, partial or provisional awards, although exhaustion of the escalation steps is excused "in the case of an emergency" without defining one. Whether an interim award compelling continued performance is enforceable in court under this clause is left open.

Either Party may "resort to court action for injunctive relief at any time," which cannot be reconciled with Section 11.1.3's stipulation that arbitration "shall be a condition precedent to any suit, action or proceeding instituted in any court." Whether and when a court may act before the arbitrator does is the question the two provisions leave.

Performance continues during a dispute "unless otherwise directed by MTC," a unilateral power given to one Party over obligations that run both ways, with no equivalent for the Network Operator and no statement of whether MTC may thereby suspend its own duties. The scope of that direction is the operative uncertainty.

The Agreement may be modified "only ... by a written document signed by both Parties," yet Section 4.7.5.2 lets Price Caps be updated annually on MTC's approval and Section 7.3 binds the operator to confidentiality policies "communicated" by MTC from time to time. The integration and no-oral-modification rule cannot be given full effect alongside those provisions.

Excuse for the other Party's fault is limited to "nonmonetary obligations," so the operator's payments remain due even where MTC's delay caused the shortfall, subject only to the narrow relief in Section 4.9.2.8. Whether that section is the exclusive monetary relief is the question left open.

Survival is limited to Articles 9 and 11 and "any other provisions that by their terms cannot be performed prior to the expiration or earlier termination," a formula that does not say whether Section 3.6 (dark fiber rights), Article 7 (post-termination confidentiality) or the seven-year record retention duties survive. The catch-all and the specific list pull against each other.

Interest accrues at "three (3) percentage points above the rediscount rate then charged by the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston," a rate no longer published under that name. The reference index may be incapable of ascertainment.

An invalid provision is "deemed to be restated to reflect the Parties' original intentions as nearly as possible," which asks a court to rewrite rather than sever. What the restated term would be is left wholly at large.

The permitted assignees are "another entity of the Commonwealth, a subsidiary of MTC or a special purpose entity," but the notice sentence then speaks of MTC assigning "to an Affiliate," a category not used in the permission and defined differently in Section 2.2. Which assignments are permitted and which require notice do not line up.

"Nothing in this Agreement shall be deemed to confer rights on any person not a Party," yet Section 10.3 requires MassDOT and its bond trustees and mortgagees to be named additional insureds and Section 9.1 extends indemnity to Affiliates, officers and agents. Whether those non-parties may enforce anything is a question the clause creates.

Clause (e) deems email notice given "when received electronically if sent by email and one of the delivery methods in (a) through (d) above," which does not say whether the email or the duplicate delivery fixes the effective date. The date of a notice sent both ways is ambiguous.

The general rule that consents "will not [be] unreasonably withheld" cannot be squared with the numerous provisions committing decisions to MTC's "sole discretion," such as Section 2.7 (revision of the CAI list), Section 4.9.7 and Section 8.2. Whether the reasonableness standard overrides those grants of discretion is unresolved.

The proviso reads "provided, however, that Network Operator shall be subject to any application or access fees," which contradicts the concessive structure of the sentence and appears to omit a negative, and the final sentence assigns the operator sole responsibility for approvals for Alterations "to be done by or on behalf of MTC." As written the allocation of fees and of approval responsibility is self-contradictory.

The Parties must "use all reasonable efforts to limit the rights and obligations of Network Operator" so that it is not a Grant subrecipient, an open-ended licence to curtail the very rights the Agreement confers. Which rights and obligations may be limited on that ground is unstated.

This conditions the Agreement on a parent guaranty "in a form acceptable to MTC, with a limit of liability no less than four million ($4,000,000) U.S. dollars," while the executed Guaranty Agreement is "limited to and capped at" exactly $4,000,000 and relieves the Guarantor of all further obligation once that sum is advanced. Whether the guaranteed performance obligations extend beyond that cap is the question the two documents leave open.
